utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, in front of you, to your right side, there is a sheet of paper. Would you please take this sheet of paper and look at it. On this sheet of paper, there is the Witness number 137. That's your code number. Below, there is a name. Is it your name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: This is name 69.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Witness, the first name on this sheet of paper, the first name, right under the number 137, is it your name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: My name is the first name, but I looked at this other thing, and I do apologise to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And if you look at the spelling of your name, is it spelled correctly?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked this because, in the various statements that the witness gave previously, it's spelled differently. That is why I asked this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And below your name, is there your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Yes, my date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Josanica, municipality of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I'm an ethnic Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was your profession before the war? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Before the war, I was a worker by profession.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you married and do you have children?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I'm married. I have four daughters.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you live before the war; in which neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Before the war, I lived in the village of Josanica, and in 1986, I bought a house in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in which neighbourhood did you live when the war broke out, that is, in April 1992? Where did you live?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: In April, when the war broke out, I was in Foca at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And in which neighbourhood of Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of the war, were you a member of any of the newly-formed parties?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I did not belong to any party before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: No, I did not have a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when the war broke out in Foca in April 1992, did you participate in the fighting at any time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: They arrested me in the house of Zahir Sandal. I was in the street of [redacted] for five days during the first war [as interpreted] when the shooting started in Foca

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When were you arrested? On what date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: They arrested me on the 13th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on that day, where were you? Were you at home or were you at someone else's house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I was in Hilmo Celo's house then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why were you not at home but in Hilmo Celo's house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Well, when the shooting started the first day, I went to his place. [redacted], and I went to his place to see whether he had gone somewhere. He had broken his leg.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who arrested you at Celo's house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Some kind of military police came, seven of them. They were in military uniform, and they said to us then that we all had to get out of that house regardless of whether we could move or not, regardless of whether there were any women and children. We all had to go to this one house, and that was Zahir Sandal's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was this house also in the Cohodar Mahala neighbourhood? Was it close to Celo's house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: It was near Celo's house and [redacted] this house was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was the owner of the house a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that all who were actually in Celo's house were taken to Sandal's house. How many people were actually taken to Sandal's house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: There were about 55 of us in Sandal's house, men, women, and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we've come across a problem there that we've had before in this trial about in-laws. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: [redacted]. It's a problem with the language, I understand. Is it important?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Let's leave it stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's a relative, and that should be enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, what ethnicity did those persons in Sandal's house have, these 55 of you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: All of these persons were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Sandal's house?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: We stayed in Sandal's house for four days.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: While you were there, were you guarded by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Well, we were guarded, but I knew some of them. They were neighbours. Nobody touched us. Nobody mistreated us. They just did their duty. There were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were you taken next?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: After that, they took us to the KP Dom, on the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who took you there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: The same troops who brought us there, they took us. They said, "Follow us." They said women and children could go home and the men had to go with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how many men were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: That group, there were -- I cannot tell you exactly, but it was around 12 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how were you taken to the KP Dom; in which vehicle?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: We were taken -- there was a bus parked there belonging to Focatrans of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The driver, was he a civilian or was he also a military person?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: He was a civilian, but believe it or not, in my fear at that time, I didn't even recognise the driver. He was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The soldiers who took you to the KP Dom, did they tell you why you were taken there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: They didn't tell us anything as to why they were taking us. They just lined us up, conducted a search to see what we had on us, what we didn't have. They took us straight to the bus then, and the bus was perhaps 10 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I was at the KP Dom from the 17th of April until the 12th of June. The 12th or the 11th of June. This month of November, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just -- you said the 11th -- 12th or 11th of June. Which year?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It seems the witness is inversing the figures for day and month.

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: It wasn't June. It was November or December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You see the note from the interpreters there. Perhaps he's been living in America for some time. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you arrived at the KP Dom on that first day, did you see soldiers at the KP Dom itself?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: We saw the soldiers who took us to the KP Dom. They didn't beat us on the way. They didn't mistreat us. They turned us over to other soldiers at the KP Dom. The other one started taking our personal details, searching us to see what we carried on us, but those who had taken us there left.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see members of the regular prison staff on your arrival on that day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: On that day, I didn't see any of the regulars. They just brought us, took our personal details, then they took us to our rooms. I didn't see any special staff on that day. Some soldiers, those who brought us, they left at that point and we were taken over by other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the regular prison staff take over from the soldiers at one point in time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Yes. They took over. They were gathering some papers when they brought us and then we were accommodated in rooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did the regular prison staff start to work in the KP Dom? When did you see the normal guards?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Well, first of all, for 10 or 15 days, the military were with us. They gave us some food, canned food, and then the civilians took over, the police. We didn't see the army any longer there. I don't know where they went.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where were you taken within the KP Dom? Do you know into which room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: They placed us in rooms. I was in Room 11. There was a central warehouse just below my room. My room was Room 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Room 11?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I stayed there until July 1993 -- sorry, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And were you then transferred to another room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: After that, I was transferred to Room 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where was this? Was it in the same building as Room 11 or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: No, it's not in the same building. It was a different room, upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the next building, you mean? You said it was in a different building. Was it in the adjacent building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: It was a different building, and we were on an upper floor when I went to Room 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you interrogated while in the prison?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Interrogation began first with some papers, documentation, and then interrogation started immediately in the evening. They brought some papers which were brought by the guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let us speak about your own interrogation first. When were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I was interrogated after 55 days. I was maybe the last from that building where there were four rooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ask to be interrogated?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, since I was the last one to remain there without having been interrogated, I was on good terms with Risto Ivanovic, the best policeman there was there. We were neighbours before the war. We knew each other well. I approached him once and asked him. I was very concerned about what would happen before I was interrogated, and he said he would look up something in some books downstairs. And the second time -- the next time he was on shift, he told me that he had looked up the books, and he said I was going to be transferred. It seemed that they had forgotten all about me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the guard mentioned is listed under number 9 in P-3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were you interrogated; in which building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: The interrogation was conducted downstairs, near the gate. You go through the gate, then you go to a room straight by the gate.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you speak about the gate, you mean this metal door leading from the yard into the administration building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Precisely. Towards the metal door, and that is where statements were taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And when you had passed the metal door, did you have to turn to the right to get to the interrogation room? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I turned right. When I went upstairs, I turned right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said you went then upstairs. How many floors upstairs?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't remember. It may have been the first floor. It may have been the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who took you there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: When I gave my statement, a policeman escorted me. He was there with us at the KP Dom. He was a certain Predo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have already heard from other witnesses that Predo is Predrag Stefanovic and he is listed under number 22 on that same P-3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you beaten on you way to the interrogation room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: There was Zoran Vladicic there. I don't know whether everyone gave their statements to him. I gave mine after 55 days. I knew that man from before the war because I worked with his father in the same enterprise. But we spent a lot of time talking on that occasion. He jumped from his chair twice as if he was going to hit me, but he didn't. There was a lot of mistreatment, but he didn't hit me. He asked me where I worked. I said I worked in Perucica enterprise of Foca, and he said,"You don't work there. I know all the stuff in that company." And in my fear at that moment, I said, "Just think of all the stuff that I unloaded together with your father and how can you be doing this to me?" He looked me in the eyes, and he grinned, and that's where the statement-taking ended. He proffered a paper to me and said, "Sign it."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I had asked you -- my brief question was actually were you beaten on the way from your room to the interrogation room? Were you beaten or hit on your way?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: They beat me when this Predo, the policeman, took me out. Downstairs there was Miro Burilo. He was at the gate. He said, "Stop." I got very frightened. I raised my hands. He hit me twice. I fell to the ground. The policeman who was escorting me lifted me by the hand and we continued on our way, and we went to Zoran's office. And if I may also add, once again in the compound, in the courtyard, I was hit when we were coming back from lunch. Some soldiers came up and hit me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, we'll go step-by-step. We do not want to mix incidents. You said that Burilo hit you twice. Did he do that in the --

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Twice. Miro Burilo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And did he beat you within the building or in the compound?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: No. He hit me when I was on my way to give my statement at Zoran Vladicic's office. He was standing at the gate.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean that he hit you after you had passed through the metal door or before?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Before I passed through the door. When I reached the metal door, when I reached him, he said, "Hands up." I raised my hands. Then he searched me. I didn't even have a comb or a handkerchief at that moment. He frisked me and he hit me twice, and the other one lifted me and said, "Nothing bad's going to happen to you."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Burilo is listed under number 56 on P-3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to your interrogation, I would like to know if Mr. Vladicic was the only person present during the interrogation or was there someone else in the room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I couldn't really say. There was another man at the office where Vladicic worked. He didn't say anything to me. I was giving my statement to Zoran. I didn't know that man who was standing at some distance, and I knew Zoran from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this other person, did he wear civilian clothes or military clothes or police clothes? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he was in civilian uniform, the other one who was standing there on the other side. I didn't know him, and he never addressed me anyway. I was just giving my statement to Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And after the interrogation was finished, did Mr. Vladicic say anything to you or to the guard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: When I finished, when I had been interrogated by Zoran Vladicic, this policeman Predo asked, "What are we going to do with him?" He said, "Take him to Room 11. He is okay."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On this particular day, was anyone else being interrogated before or after you in the same room or in the adjacent rooms?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I cannot remember that because I was the last one to stay in that building before being interrogated. I didn't see anyone else going to interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you have already started to describe how you were beaten in the yard. When were you beaten in the yard later?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Once when we were going to lunch or breakfast or supper, sometimes they would let out one or two rooms at the same time or even three rooms, and to tell you honestly, when we were going back, some of the people would grab some grass from the lawn and the guards would run after us angrily and hit us. Sometimes I got hit and other people got hit too. This Burilo, he called us "motherfuckers" and cursed us and cursed our mother.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, were you ever beaten by soldiers when you passed through the yard?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. An entire sentence is missing from the transcript. When the witness said that it was only when he went to Kalinovik that he experienced, and I don't want to repeat his words here. Perhaps my learned friend could repeat the question. The witness was saying that at the KP Dom, he experienced what he experienced, and it was only at Kalinovik that he really had it bad and that wasn't recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understand where you suggest the qualification should be inserted in the answer. Was it in the course of the answer or the beginning or the end or where?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just behind 22 and 23, it says, "Our mother," and then continues the sentence which I am saying is missing, which means line 23 on page 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: At the end of the answer as it is recorded. And what were the words which you say were used?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. We really didn't get all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're getting nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think there is another mistake because in the transcript the witness said Burilo and it was actually the soldiers. That is one thing. And another thing, after this sentence there should come what I just mentioned. He experienced in the KP Dom only those unpleasant things that he experienced, but he really had it bad only in Kalinovik, and that's what he mentioned happened to him. I don't want to repeat the whole sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I think the best thing to do would be to ask him a series of questions to try and get the whole of that out. The interpreters concede that they missed part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It was quite a long answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you said that detainees were beaten in the yard, and you among them as well. Who beat you in the yard in the KP Dom? We are only talking about the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I don't know who hit me. They were in military clothing. Five or six of them would come down on us when we were coming from breakfast. The guards there were driving us hard to get into the building as fast as we can. Five or six soldiers came down on us who were standing around. Sometimes they would hit us; sometimes they wouldn't. Once I got hit a couple of times. Other people fared worse because they couldn't go faster. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when did this happen that soldiers beat you and other detainees? Was it in the beginning of your defence or later? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: That is -- that was in the beginning, in the first months. In April.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what were the soldiers doing in the yard? Why were they there? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: To tell you honestly, I don't know what they were doing down there in the compound and whether they were coming to the canteen or whether they were doing some work there. I didn't know anyone, and I didn't know what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That might be an appropriate place to break. Mr. Bakrac, it may be best if you obtained that concession by way of cross-examination. I don't think the Prosecution needs to go into that, but you certainly may, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, just a remark. I will also ask him a few questions about Kalinovik, and I am aware that he will say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Okay. We'll resume at 3.00 --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.30 p.m. 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He has no earphones on. Can you help him with the earphones?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, you told us how you were beaten in the yard on one occasion, and I have just a few more questions related to this. The hits that you received on this occasion, were they heavy blows?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, this was in the beginning, the first month. When the soldiers were with us, then we were hit. I was hit once. Others were hit several times because it varied from room to room. That was during the first month while the soldiers were with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And my question was: Did those blows that you received on this one occasion, did it hurt you? Were they heavy blows?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Oh, well, a blow or two. Well, he hit you as much as he could and not whether it hurt you or not. Well ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was it painful?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Well, it was painful. Let's say it was supposed to be painful.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you recall anybody else by name who was beaten as well, any of the other detainees who were beaten with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: No. This was according to groups, sometimes when people would go out to breakfast or lunch or when they were older people who couldn't go out for meals. Then also sometimes we would be pushed into our rooms, to get into them as soon as possible. This was the month of April while the soldiers were with us, while we ate military cans.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were guards, regular prison guards present when that happened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Well, they tried to put us away. There were good ones among them who were trying to put us away, shelter us, who told us, "Go into the rooms. They won't go into the rooms." There were good men among the guards who said that to us. For example, if it were Risto Ivanovic's shift, he would get us into the rooms even before our time was up.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said good men among the guards helped in a way. What about the bad men among the guards? Were there such men too?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Well, what I can tell you is that no matter how many statements are given, the number of people that Burilo beat up can only be bigger than that. Not only me. It's not only the people who gave statements that were beaten up by Burilo. Whereas among the policemen, there were some who did not say a bad word to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, did the guards -- when those beatings in the yard occurred, did the soldiers ever stop the guards from beating the detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Well, he didn't stop them. They just said to us, "If you see they are coming towards you, run to your rooms and get into your rooms as soon as you can." They didn't dare stop them and tell them not to beat us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this incident and this kind of incident are part of 5.11 in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, were detainees beaten in the administration building? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I didn't really understand what you said well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were detainees beaten in the administration building, in particular, in the evenings?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: In the evenings? There were no beatings in the evening. There was a roll-call at 8.00 in the evening so that they could see how many of us are in each room, so that they could see whether we were all there. But then, all of a sudden later, guards brought in some papers and then they would tell some people to go out to make a statement. They would take two or three persons from each room, for instance, and then they would go out there to give those statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did this occur throughout your detention or was it only in a certain period of time? When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that that was in a certain period of time. Somebody wrote some kind of papers. I don't know. This went through papers. I don't know. It was the end of April, the month of May, and then it was through these papers and then it sort of calmed down. It was slower then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you speak of papers. What kind of papers were they? Were they lists or notes? Did you ever have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: No. I did manage to see the papers. The policeman on duty would always bring a paper and call out such-and-such a name, and then he'd say, "Come on, you're coming with me to give a statement."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you see where the selected detainees were taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: These detainees, they were taken straight to the gate where the assembly room was, towards the gate.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Were they taken through the metal door?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 16, a part seems to be missing. When the witness said there, where we went to give statements. It only says here, "through that door," and the witness added something to his sentence, "Where we went to make statements."

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I wouldn't know about this metal door. We went there to make statements. That's where people were taken. It was in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm still trying to find the expression "through the door." Line 16, to which you refer, is "towards the gate," and the question was, "Yes. Were they taken through the metal door?" What do you say it should have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of the sentence, the witness said what he repeated just now for the transcript, that these people were taken to where statements were being given. That's what he said earlier on, and he repeated that now in the transcript, Your Honour. So that was the end of the sentence. "Towards the metal door," and then they were taken to where statements were given. That is the part that's missing from the transcript, and the witness seems to have explained it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you think it's important, at least it's now been recorded. You proceed, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the detainees were out of your view, could you hear any sounds of beatings or screaming?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: We heard this when they were taking these groups out. Sounds were coming from this assembly room where they had been taken; staff room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where was this assembly room or staff room? Where was it in the building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: That room was near number 11 from the first building.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the photo 7477.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, if you look at this photo, does this look familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I cannot orient myself here. What I know here is that there was Room 11 below the central warehouse. Do you have a photograph of the central warehouse? My room, Room 11, was right above it, right above the central warehouse. As for this photograph, I don't know if you understand what I'm telling you, but I cannot orient myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the photo 7473.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does this look familiar to you? Can you orient yourself? Would you please look at the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Give the photo to the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Please have a look at this photo. When you see what it shows --

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I see the building of the KP Dom. However, the only thing I know is that my room was above the central warehouse. I've been looking at this photograph, perhaps you've got one too, but really, I cannot orient myself now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This assembly room that you spoke about, is it in the same building where your room was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: No, it was not in the same building. It was not in the same building. It was separate here. Building number 11 and the assembly room was here. Whether it was over there from the exit door, the outside door, I don't know, but some -- before the war, detainees -- prisoners received visitors there through that assembly room. I passed through that assembly room when I went to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have clarified now, and I think everybody understands now where the room is that you're talking about. You need not look at photographs any longer.

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I don't know if you understand what I'm telling you. I can't really see much in these things, but if you could show me the central warehouse, I think I ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, that wouldn't really help because we're talking about the assembly room and not about the room where you were. It's okay. It's cleared. Thank you. Witness, can you tell us the names of detainees that you remembered that were called out from your room and taken away to this assembly room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I can say that they were taken in smaller groups in the month of May. It may have spilled over into June as well. Esad Soro Halilovic, Kemo Dzelilovic, Nail Hodzic, Mustafa Kuloglija. Uzunovic Enes, Seval Soro, Alija Altoka, and -- I had a list here. If you allow me, perhaps I haven't mentioned two men.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, before you use your list, I would like to know, when did you make the list?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I had made this list earlier on too so that I would know that these people were with me, if we ever survived. However, nothing doing. All of that was thrown away when we went to Kalinovik. Even our handkerchiefs and shoelaces were thrown away, everything. Then the bags we carried. When I found out that I was supposed to come here, I had to remember the people who were taken out during the night. I believe that my other colleagues who will be coming here will not deny that about these men.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, please take your list. Do you have the notes with you, this list that you just spoke about?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I have got some notes. Please will you allow me to look at them? I may have made a mistake with regard to, say, two men.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, just use the list --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, this list containing 11 names was distributed to all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We still don't know when he made it, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to clarify this with you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That would be, I think, preferable.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This particular list, Witness, which is now in front of you, when did you write it? When?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I had made that list earlier on, earlier on, if I would ever find anything out about these people, whether these people are alive or not alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Again we have a mistake of substance in the transcript. The witness said, "I made this mistake earlier on too," but he said he made it earlier on too, and that is a big mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't see what the substance in this is at all. All we're asking him for, with some difficulty getting an answer, is when he wrote it. That's all we want to know. These answers, so far, are totally irrelevant to anything. Now, just let us find out when he wrote it, about when, and if there is some problem that arises out of that, you can raise it. But if there was something left out in one of his answers, I can assure you they are totally useless to us in this trial. Now, sir, please, will you tell us, when did you sit down and write this list out? What year was it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: The year was 1992, when I was in Foca, when these people were taken out. That was in 1992. However, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. That's enough. That's all we want to have at the moment. Now, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you want to tender it, do you?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but I think there is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This list, Witness, in front of you, did you make it after your release from the KP Dom? This list, did you make it after your release?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I did not. I just repeated this list when I was released from the KP Dom. I made a list to see whether everything was the same, whether everything corresponded so that if I would come here, I wanted to see whether all these people I had written before matched this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So this list that you have now in your hand you produced after your release, but it's a similar one that you made during your time in the KP Dom. Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Of course. Right. That's it. It's not that I expressed myself that way, but that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in which year did you make this duplicate list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think you'd better try again, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have told us that in the KP Dom you made a list, but this list was actually taken away from you, but the names you remembered and you wrote down after your release. When did you write it down after your release?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I wrote this list when I was exchanged in Trnovo. Let me repeat these people's names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment. You've just got to answer the questions. We'll get nowhere if you keep on trying to say something you haven't been asked about. What year were you released?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I was released in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And how long after you were released did you write out this duplicate list or what you say is a duplicate list?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I wrote it sometime when I got home, perhaps within a month's time. I was always thinking about the list that had to do with my statement. I always thought I'd go to a court, because my first list was thrown away when I left Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I think we've got approximate date of when it was written.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And I would like to enter this into evidence and then discuss number -- name by name with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Has it got an ID number?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection to the list, Mr. Bakrac? You can ask him about his mistakes later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I just want to explain that my objection was in the following direction: That there were two lists, and that's the difference in that mistake; "this list too." However, never mind. Before the Defence says what it has to say, it would like to have a look at the original that the witness is holding in his hand. So could the usher help us and let us have a look at the list that the witness is holding in his hand right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean the original of which this is a photostat copy. He doesn't pretend to have the original list, the one that he wrote in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, then the list he has in his hands right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You want to see it. Any objection, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Usher, would you please take it from the witness and show it to Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And just for the information for the Court, I saw this list during the conference, before, when he came here, and I made these copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Some people may have an overcautious approach to these things, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, but I think the Defence is entitled to do it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence wanted to see whether this paper was nine years old. However, that is going to be a subject of our cross-examination. This is not a photocopy. This is the original. We do not object to having this piece of paper admitted into evidence. The usher can return this to the witness. However, the witness has another piece of paper in front of him, and the Defence would like to know what that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think as long as we do not discuss the matter of the other papers he has, I think there's no reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He may have a letter from his mother. What's it got to do with you at this stage? If he uses it for the purposes of refreshing his recollection, that's a completely different thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seemed to me that the witness was holding this piece of paper in his hands because he wanted to refresh his memory. Of course, I don't want to go into his personal letters or am I interested in that, but he held this piece of paper as if he wanted to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You are not only an expert on the age of paper but also you can read minds, I gather, Mr. Bakrac. Anyway, wait until he wants to use it for the purposes of refreshing his recollection. Then we will inquire as to what it is. At the moment, this is Exhibit P444. Now, is there a need for any of these names to be under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's actually people from Schedule C and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I recognise a few of the names, anyway. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, please take the list with the 11 names, and please tell us what you saw happen to Mr. Nail Hodzic, the first name on your list. Please use your list. Open it. Open your list and look at it.

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I can say only about Nail that he was taken away. He was taken away by the policemen from the KP Dom. He said, "Nail, come out to give a statement," and he said, "Brothers, what are you doing? What have I got to do with statements?" and he said, "Nail, you'll be right back. You're just supposed to give a statement." So this Nail perhaps went there two or three times and then, all of sudden, he was taken away and never returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Hodzic return from one of these interrogations with injuries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: In that sadness, I could not walk up to him to see whether he had any injuries. The man returned from there sad. He came back twice or three times, and then the last time he didn't return.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person Nail Hodzic is mentioned under B-28 and C-10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Kemo Dzelilovic, was he taken once, twice, or how often?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Kemo Dzelilovic, too, was taken out in that time frame two or three times, and the only thing we noticed -- I noticed when he came back once. Vahida Dzemo, he was a policeman before in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you. You were just speaking about Kemo Dzelilovic, and all I heard is that you said you noticed something.

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Oh, you mean Kemo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. You said you noticed something when he returned. What did you notice?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: We noticed some blows on him, this Kemo Dzelilovic. I didn't ask him who had hit him, nor did he tell us. Some yelling could be heard from outside, and once when they came to pick him up, one night, how he turned out, I don't know. However, none of them has been heard from since, none of those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's B-19 and C-7 for Kemo Dzelilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have started with Dzemo Vahida. Was he taken out on several occasions as well?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Yes. Dzemo Vahida, I can tell you sincerely that I saw him when he was returned. He was a policeman in Foca. He was holding his own head with his hands. He said he had been hit -- kicked in the head. I don't know what had happened to him exactly, but he was holding his hand on his face and he said two of his teeth were broken.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dzemo Vahida is in the indictment in the incident 5.29 and also on Schedule C, number 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mustafa Kuloglija. What can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: About him, I couldn't tell you anything. He was taken away in the same groups in the evening. He used to reside in Aladza, where he had an apartment, in Foca. I knew him as a good neighbour. He left during the night. He wasn't even in the same room with me. He was in the room next door. But when he left, he never returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is C-15 and B-34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Alija Altoka. Was he in your room, and what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Alija Altoka was in my room. He had a father by the name of Omer. He was in my room. He was a young man, a boy practically, perhaps the youngest of all the people I've mentioned. He was taken on the same journey, and he -- well, the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said he was the youngest among you. How old was he, approximately?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: He was about 30 years old. Of all the people that I have mentioned here, he was the youngest of those boys, young men.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's C-1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have listed under number 6 Soro Dzevad, but you have crossed him out. Why is he on the list and why did you cross him out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I crossed this man out. He didn't leave then during the night when those others were taken. This man, Dzevad Soro, was with me in the same room when I was transferred to Room 18 sometime in end July.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the next person is Soro Seval. What can you tell us about him? Was he in your room and was he taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Seval Soro was not in my room. He was in the room next door. He was an electrician by occupation. He told us he had two children. He was also a young man, an electrician. He was also taken during the night the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he taken several times or did you see him being taken only once?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Well, from what I know about him, he was taken once and he wasn't returned, this Seval Soro who was an electrician by occupation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is listed under C-15 and B-54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The next person, Munib Veiz, was he in your room, and what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Munib Veiz. He wasn't in my room either. He was in a neighbouring room. He was a trader, a salesperson. He worked in a leather shop near the bazaar. He was a big, fat man. Once he returned beaten up so badly that we had to feed him like a chicken. We brought him the soup, the little soup we could find, and some bread. We didn't even dare ask him who had beat him up. He was suffering something terrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this Munib Veiz is listed under B-59 and C-28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The next person, Meho Sofradzija, was he in your room, and what can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: About Meho Sofradzija, I can tell you that he was not in my room either. I heard his voice only once when somebody was interrogating him out there. He said -- he was asked what had happened, and he just cried for help, something like, "Dear mother, help me." It was nothing. And the person insisted. I wasn't the only one heard it. Others heard it too when he was saying, "I didn't have any. I didn't have any," and the other person said, "Your neighbours said you did," and he said, "I didn't." He was taken out in one of the groups when people were taken out by four or five from a room and that's how he went.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you know him so well that you could recognise his voice?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that man from the civilian days. He was not far away from me. I knew him from civilian days. I knew he worked in the town hall in some institution. That's where he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is listed under B-52.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Next, you had listed Reko Rasim. Who is that, and what can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Rasim Reko. He, too, was a neighbour of mine. He lived close to me, from Josanica or some place. He worked at the carpenter's shop of the KP Dom. I don't know about his beatings. All I know is he was taken out one evening. I didn't hear his voice. I didn't hear him screaming or defending himself. I knew him. He was working at the carpentry of the KP Dom where furniture was produced.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is not on any of the schedules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the last person from your list is Enes Uzunovic. Was he in your room or what can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: As for Enes Uzunovic, I didn't know this man. He was in my room, though. He had something -- there was something wrong with him. He was pulling at his hair and crying for help all the time. The first month when they were still allowing visits, in April, he was returned. He couldn't see the wife and children who were allowed to see him, and he kept crying all the time. What was wrong with him, I don't know. I didn't even know the man.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see him return to the room with injuries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I didn't notice any injuries. All I remember, all that I noticed when we had this visit is that he was returned from the gate. His wife and daughter were going towards him and wanted to hug him, but they didn't allow him to meet them. He was returned from the gate then. And he later disappeared like other people disappeared at certain intervals.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person is listed under C-26 and 5.29 in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a Jusuf Dzamalija?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Juso Dzamalija, [redacted]. [redacted]. He came to the isolation cell. It was not only me. Many people saw him when he came into the isolation cell. Several days later, Juso Dzamalija was carried out of the isolation cell in a blanket. Whether he had killed himself or he was killed, whether he survived, I don't know. All I know is that, three months later, he was carried out in a blanket. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Three months later after what? After what he was brought in or what?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question? I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that, "All I know is that, three months later, he was carried out in a blanket," and my question was: Three months later after what?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I made a mistake. It was not three months. He had been there several days. I knew the man well. We had worked together. But I want to tell you what I know. Rumour had it that this man had killed himself in the isolation cell. How much truth there is in this claim, I don't know. Maybe he killed himself, maybe he was killed, but that's the story that circulated about this person.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you see him being carried out in a blanket?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I could see through a small window when he was carried out. Whether he had committed suicide or was killed, whether he was dead at all, I don't know. All I know is that he was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who carried him? Was it guards or who? Who carried him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: The guards carried him out then. What happened to him, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you recognise his body or him in the blanket? Did you see him actually in the blanket?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I did see him on the blanket, but I was at some distance, looking through the window. He was in that isolation cell. I remember when he went there, and I remember when he was returned. Whether he was on that blanket dead or alive, what he had done to himself, I don't know. All I know is that he worked in Perucica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, what I wanted to know is did you recognise him when he was carried in the blanket? Did you actually see his body or him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Yes. I swear I did recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was the warden in the KP Dom? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: About the warden of the KP Dom, I can say I didn't know the warden of the KP Dom before the war. I didn't even meet him in the KP Dom. Only when the visits were allowed in the first month, in April, my daughter and wife came to visit me, to see me. They were brought by a Serb neighbour in a car. They passed through. They came to see me. They were at the door. I don't remember which door it was. Somebody asked them, "Who do you want to see?" They said -- my daughter said, "I want to see my dad." They said, "You can't." Then they started crying. There was the guard on duty, Risto Ivanovic, who knew me and my daughter, and he said to her, "Come on. Come on, girl. The warden is only joking. Why are you crying?" And she said, "The warden said I couldn't see you." And this daughter of mine, she knew him from before the war, from school.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me just go into some more details. Who was the warden? Can you tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I know that in the beginning of the war, the warden was Milorad Krnojelac. When he was replaced, at what time, whether it was in the summer or not or which year, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you met your daughter, when you could see your daughter and your wife, what exactly did your daughter tell you about meeting the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: My daughter said, when she came to me, "Why are you crying?" And she says, "The warden wouldn't let me come through." And this neighbour, Ivanovic, who knew her, patted her on the shoulder and said, "Come through. Come through, girl. The warden is probably joking." And then if you bring 300 prisoners here, they will all confirm that he was, from the beginning of the war, that he was warden and what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did your daughter, when she spoke about the warden, did she mention the name of Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Yes. They knew each other in school.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when your daughter was talking to you, did she actually mention that the warden was Mr. Krnojelac? What did she say? Try to remember what exactly she said.

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: She said -- when she came to me, she was crying. I asked, "What's the matter with you?" And she said, "The warden of the KP Dom wouldn't let me through just now," and this neighbour, Risto Ivanovic, patted her on the shoulder and said, "Come through, girl. The warden is probably just joking."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you hear from anyone else that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden or was this your only reference?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I heard -- I once already told you, no matter how many witnesses you bring -- but the thing is, I don't know how long he was warden, until when, and when he was replaced. But until he was replaced, he was the warden in that month. It was the April, when the war started.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, I had asked you - and please answer my question - who else besides your daughter mentioned that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I think that all the statements that exist here from prisoners, I believe all of them said that he was the warden.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, did the guards ever mention that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: They didn't tell me. These guards, they had no conflicts with me. They just took me in or out whenever necessary. We had no particular communication with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you gave a statement to the Prosecutor's office. Do you remember that? It was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: 1996? I don't remember that I mentioned anything then, because I wasn't in the KP Dom then at all. I was exchanged in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, I was asking you, did you give a statement to the Prosecutor's office, to investigators, after your release?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Most probably I gave a statement, I gave that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me please cite from your statement, and it's page 4, paragraph 4 -- sorry, first paragraph in the English version, and it's the same in the B/C/S version. "During my detention at KP Dom, I have never met Milorad Krnojelac. The name sounds familiar to me. I heard the guard mentioning him. They were looking for him to solve problems. During my stay, I have never met or heard about Savo Todovic." Does this jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Whether you believe it or not, I have no complete data at all about Slavko Todovic because I never heard anything about that man. How he performed his duties, what he did, what he represented, I have no clue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. We were not talking about Slavko Todovic, we were talking about Mr. Krnojelac, and at least in your previous statement, you mentioned that you heard guards mentioning him when a problem had to be solved. Do you recall anything like this, or don't you remember any longer?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I cannot remember that. I only remember what my daughter said about knowing him from school when she came in April to visit me. As for these events, I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it may be relevant that he said he'd never heard of Mr. Todovic either in his statement as to what weight we give to the previous one, but your question that you've put to him does not put that fact into evidence. I'm only drawing your attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I was coming to Mr. Todovic and Mr. Rasevic next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, but you've just put it to him that's what his statement says. There is no evidence before us that's what his statement does say, and it may be you need to follow the procedure we've now adopted by asking the Defence, at the appropriate stage, to accept that that is in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I can do it right now, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you like, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, Mr. Vasic, do you accept that what I just read is in the statement, this paragraph about Mr. Krnojelac and about him never hearing or meeting Slavko Todovic? The reference was page 4, first paragraph in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think you'll have to ask in relation to both statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is only one statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. Both statements -- I'm sorry. Both sentences in that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What you read out before was: "During my detention at KP Dom, I never met Milorad Krnojelac. The name sounds familiar to me. I heard the guard mentioning him. They were looking for him to solve problems. During my stay, I've never met or heard about Savo Todovic." You seek to have a concession from the Defence that that appeared in this witness's statement that he gave to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As my learned friend read it out, that is the same thing that is written in his statement which we have received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned already that you do not know Savo Todovic, and you cannot say what function he had. Do you know Mitar Rasevic and his function?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: About Todovic, I guarantee to you with my life that I don't know anything. And as for Rasevic, they said he was the police commander there, Mitar Rasevic, that he was commander of the police at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you see him in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him a couple of times. He didn't hit me. He didn't say anything to me. He would sometimes come on inspection tours, when roll-calls were made. He was together with a policeman on duty. I remember one case in August when a lot of people were taken out, taken to pick some fruit, they explained to those people that, "You're going to work. You're going to pick fruit. Don't take too many things." There was a policeman called Pasovic. They took those people away. Where they went, I don't know. All I know is that those people are missing today. Not a single one of them reappeared that I know of. For this fruit picking, they were taken out in broad daylight, according to the list they brought with them. There were only young men on that list.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Thank you, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you were detained until November or December 1992. Where were you taken from KP Dom; to which place?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I was taken from the camp in Foca to the KP Dom at Kalinovik. There were 13 other men. We got this piece of information: "You're going for an exchange." The policeman on duty in the morning, he said, "You're going out for an exchange. I'm now going to take care of breakfast, together with the other detainees, and you get your things ready. You'll be the last to have breakfast, and after breakfast, I'm going to take you to the gate and then there will be a roll-call waiting for you."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this group of 13 people that you mentioned that were taken together with you, was there the person who is listed under the number 69 on this sheet of paper in front of you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Yes. That person number 69 was there. I guarantee that with my own life and my own head.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, who took you to Kalinovik? Was it the soldiers or the guards?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I can say that the guards did not take us. The guard who was with us only took us to the gate, and he said, "Wait for the roll-call." Then the roll-call happened. One by one, as the roll-call went on, we started going out. There was this Land Rover there, and we were getting into the Land Rover one by one. Who had an extra shirt or extra clothes or whatever could not take it. They could only go to Kalinovik wearing the trousers and the shirts we had. They even made us take shoelaces out of our shoes. If we had any, they made us throw them out. There were military soldiers there and then there was the Land Rover and there was the James there, the James with the tarpaulin. We were enclosed in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The James, is that a kind of truck or what is a James?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: A truck, a military truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on your way to Kalinovik, were you mistreated?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: On the road to Kalinovik, I can say that we were beaten badly. We came to Kalinovik. I could not recognise these people. They were -- they were soldiers, quite tall, yellowish, and there was some kind of police and this Land Rover, and there were four with us up on the vehicle. They threw away all our things. We came to Kalinovik at the worst time, during the winter, and we only wore trousers and shirts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you stay in Kalinovik? In which particular place?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: In Kalinovik, we were put up at some kind of a military warehouse, an abandoned warehouse within a compound. We came there. They opened the vehicle. We couldn't even walk down those two or three steps. They had to take us by the hand and throw us out there as if we were logs. We stayed there. We had no conditions there whatsoever as compared to Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Kalinovik, in this military warehouse?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: You know what? There were people there. One week there would be one exchange. The police would come from the MUP and they would take one, and they'd say nicely, "You're going out for an exchange." There was only one day when two men were taken out. But there were some people there who even stayed for three months. I was the fourth person there. When I was exchanged from Kalinovik, then three of my colleagues remained there, and the exchanges were extinguished.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when were you exchanged, on what day? Do you know that? Or what month?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I was exchanged from Kalinovik. I was exchanged on the 9th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you were arrested in April 1992, were you a healthy man?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Your Honour, I swear on my mother's grave that I had been in good health. I was not beaten too much in the house. All the beatings we got, we got at Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, when you left the KP Dom -- we're speaking about -- now in steps. When you left the KP Dom, what was your physical condition at that time? Yes. When you left the KP Dom in November or December 1992, what was your physical condition?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: My health condition? I'm not going to lie to you. I swear by my mother and by my children, when I left from Foca -- I mean, before, my health was good, but when I left from Kalinovik, when I went home --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We're not talking about Kalinovik now. I want to know how was your condition when you left Foca, when you left the KP Dom? Did you have physical effects from the confinement at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Maybe something small or physical. Some of these effects from Foca, no, but all of the effects came later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And what was your physical condition when you left Kalinovik?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Well, from Kalinovik, that was really terrible. My condition after Kalinovik, that was really terrible. Until the present day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is this really relevant? I mean, we've got to stop this sort of thing. How is it relevant in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's part of the widespread and systematic conditions in the other camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, see if you can get a short answer out of him, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You had trouble to get here to testify because of your physical condition. Does this relate to Kalinovik condition, your rheumatism and your bone problems?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: All of it is from Kalinovik. All my problems were from Kalinovik, and that's why I kept putting off my coming here, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just tell us what your physical condition was, shortly, when you left Kalinovik, please.

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: Good. Pretty good. But all the effects I had, I got at Kalinovik, up there at Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what were the symptoms that you had? What was it that you suffered?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: You mean who beat us?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, the physical results. What injuries did you have? What about your rheumatism?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I had effects when I left Kalinovik. I have a bad back, I have a bad hip, I have a bad knee, I had a broken rib. All of these are the effects of Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are the questions we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't really want to reopen this, but if you're relying upon it, don't you have to show that it wasn't from falling out of a window or something?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, the conditions that you had, the broken rib, the bone problem, what caused these problems?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: We had to be injured because they stripped us naked in Kalinovik and beat us. Can I tell you now about one case? Will you listen to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, sir. No, no, please. Is that not sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I would like to introduce myself to you. I am Miroslav Vasic, attorney-at-law, one of the Defence counsel for the accused, Milorad Krnojelac. First of all, sir, tell me, in addition to this statement that my learned friend asked you about, the one that you gave to the investigators of the OTP on the 20th of June, 1996, did you give two other statements, one to the public security station on the 7th of February, 1993, and another one to the sector of state security on the 29th of July, 1994?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I remember these statements, when I gave a statement in Trnovo, when I came, and how many statements I gave, I can't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In addition to the statement you gave in Trnovo, did you give a statement on the 29th of July in 1994 in the state security centre in Gorazde? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I gave a statement in Gorazde. I gave a statement in Trnovo. I also gave a statement once when they came to my home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, when you are answering a question from the Defence counsel, because you're both speaking the same language, it is very difficult for the interpreters to keep up with you. You know how when you were answering questions from the Prosecution you waited until the translation was finished before you answered it or answered those questions. When you are speaking with Mr. Vasic here, you are both speaking the same language, but the interpreters are still translating the same question, even though he has stopped speaking. So just pause for a short period before you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: FWS-137
utterances.text: I mean all of it seemed that way to me, too, that we'd get all of this confused. This is the first trial I've ever been to in my lifetime, and this is a really big thing for me, Your Honour. I am not familiar with any of this. I -- it just came upon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We understand that. We understand you want to tell us everything, but we really are here to hear your evidence on some very narrow issues, and that's why we are trying to restrict you to that evidence or to the evidence relating to those issues. We understand that you have a lot that you would like to say. Unfortunately, we just simply are unable to hear everything you want to say.
